question: An app runs on one server and keeps sessions in a map in its own memory. The team starts a second copy, and users report being logged out at random. What is the cause?
options: Browsers drop cookies when two servers exist
The map is too small for two servers
Each copy only knows the sessions created in its own memory, so a request that reaches the other copy finds no session
HTTP forbids sessions on more than one server
explanation: In-memory sessions live in one process. When a request lands on a copy that did not create the session, the lookup fails and the user looks logged out. A shared session store fixes it.

question: After moving sessions to a shared Redis store, what happens when one of the application servers is restarted?
options: Nobody is logged out: the sessions live in Redis, and the other servers keep answering with them
Every user is logged out, because the sessions were created on that server
Only the users of that server are logged out
Redis deletes every session whenever any client disconnects
explanation: The servers are stateless: the session records live in the shared store, so a restart of one server loses nothing and any copy can answer the next request.

question: A user logs out of an app that uses JWTs valid for 7 days, with no other server-side check. An attacker copied the token earlier. What happens?
options: The token stops working at logout, because the browser deletes it
The server detects the copy because the signature changes
The token is valid for one more request only
The token keeps working until its `exp` time, because nothing on the server remembers that it was revoked
explanation: A signed token is verified with the key and the expiry only. Without a revocation list or short expiry, logout deletes the client's copy but not the attacker's.

question: A developer stores the user's email and an internal discount code in a JWT payload, reasoning that the token is signed. What is wrong?
options: Signed tokens cannot carry strings
The payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone holding the token can read it; the signature prevents changes, not reading
The server can no longer verify the signature
The token becomes stateful and needs a session store
explanation: Signing protects integrity: a changed payload fails verification. It does not hide anything, because the payload is plain JSON encoded in base64url.

question: Session ids are generated as `session-1`, `session-2` and so on. Why is that a security problem?
options: Redis cannot store keys with numbers
Cookies must contain a JWT
An attacker can guess other users' live ids and send them as their own cookie
Counters overflow after 1,000 sessions
explanation: The session id is the only proof of the login, so it must be unguessable. A cryptographically secure random id makes guessing a live session practically impossible.

question: Why give a server-side session a time-to-live even though logout already deletes it?
options: So that sessions of users who never log out, and ids that were stolen, stop working on their own
Because HTTP requires every cookie to expire within an hour
To make the servers stateful
Because Redis refuses keys without a TTL
explanation: Most users close the tab instead of logging out. A TTL bounds how long a forgotten or stolen session id is useful and keeps the store from growing forever.
